title: Gen Z Defies the Odds: How Some 20-Somethings Are Buying Homes in an Unaffordable Market
summary:
In a housing market where the average first-time buyer is 40 years old, 27-year-old Francisco Vazquez stands out. He recently purchased a three-bedroom home in Milwaukee for $220,000—nearly half the national median—after aggressively saving $72,000 in just over two years. Vazquez is part of a small but growing cohort of Gen Zers who are managing to buy homes despite historically high prices and a massive housing shortage.

Vazquez's journey required significant sacrifices. He majored in conservation science on a scholarship, then worked rescuing alligators and later at a zoo—jobs he loved but that paid too little to build a future. "I wasn't going to be able to support a wife, let alone kids, or buy a home," he said. So he moved back to Wisconsin, lived rent-free with his parents for a year, and stumbled into a fast-food management job with good pay and benefits. He was promoted twice. His strict saving plan was challenged when he started dating his now-wife, who encouraged a bit more spending on experiences. "She's definitely helped me balance," he said.

Data from the National Association of Realtors shows Gen Z buyers (ages 18–26) made up 4% of the market last year, up from 3%. They're outpacing millennials at the same age, and they're doing it differently: they're twice as likely to be single buyers, especially women, and less likely to rely on parental help. Their average household income is $76,000, and they're financially savvy, often using social media for planning. Economist Jessica Lautz notes, "Gen Zers seem to have learned from millennials."

Vazquez put down a large down payment and secured a 15-year fixed-rate mortgage. His ultimate goal? Early retirement. "Buying a home helps me buy myself more freedom in general," he said. While Gen Z homeowners remain a sliver of the market, their rise is notable given the odds: record unaffordability, vanishing starter homes, and wages that haven't kept pace. Their strategies—relocating to affordable cities, saving relentlessly, and embracing financial literacy—offer a potential roadmap for others.
why_it_matters: For teenagers starting to think about their future, this story highlights the power of deliberate financial planning and the tough trade-offs their generation may face to afford a home. It also shows that systemic problems like high housing costs don’t make homeownership impossible, but do require unusual sacrifices or relocating to less expensive cities—choices that will shape where and how they live as adults.

background_read: Homeownership among young adults has declined sharply over the last two decades as prices have risen much faster than wages. The median sale price of a home in the United States is now over $400,000, and the average first-time buyer is 40 years old. Generations are shaped by different economic shocks: millennials came of age during the 2008 financial crisis and faced a brutal job market, while Gen Z (born roughly between 1997 and 2012) is entering adulthood during a period of high inflation, after a pandemic that disrupted housing supply chains.

Milwaukee is one of several midsize, more affordable cities — others include Cleveland, Indianapolis, and Buffalo — that young buyers are targeting to avoid the extreme unaffordability of coastal metros. The National Association of Realtors is a major real-estate trade group that collects data on home sales and buyer profiles. Economists note that Gen Z is unusually financially literate, in part because they have grown up with easy access to money-management content on platforms like TikTok and YouTube. A 15-year fixed-rate mortgage, compared with a more common 30-year term, builds equity much faster and saves tens of thousands of dollars in interest, but requires higher monthly payments — a trade-off that requires both discipline and a solid income.

perspectives.description: Stories like Vazquez’s show that Gen Z can overcome a brutal housing market through aggressive saving, geographical flexibility, and financial literacy. By leveraging high-demand management jobs and avoiding student debt, some young people are carving out a path that seemed closed, offering hope that homeownership doesn’t have to be a distant dream.

The reality is that most young adults cannot move in with parents for a year, land a promotion quickly, or relocate to a cheaper city without sacrificing career opportunities. The market remains deeply unfair: wages have not kept pace with home prices, and relying on extreme personal sacrifice as a solution lets policymakers and developers off the hook for failing to build enough affordable starter homes.

This trend reflects a broader structural shift. Starter homes have virtually disappeared from many markets as investors buy up smaller properties and zoning laws restrict new construction. Gen Z’s approach — using social media for financial education, buying alone, avoiding parental dependence — suggests a pragmatic adaptation to an economy that no longer guarantees upward mobility through a standard career path.

If affordability continues to worsen, Gen Z’s homeownership rates may plateau once again, and the small gains could prove fragile. However, if the strategies seen here spread — moving to lower-cost cities, embracing non-traditional careers with fast advancement, and prioritizing financial independence — this generation could reshape housing demand and even influence where new construction and job opportunities cluster in the next decade.
